summary: The singular value decomposition says every matrix is a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation. You derive it from the eigenvectors of AᵀA, read singular values as the axes of an ellipse, and implement it two ways.
html:
Every matrix maps a circle to an ellipse

Push the unit circle through any 2 × 2 matrix and you get an ellipse (possibly flattened to a line). Its semi-axes have lengths σ1​≥σ2​≥0, the singular values, and point along perpendicular unit vectors u1​,u2​. The input directions that land on those axes, v1​,v2​, are perpendicular too. So

Avi​=σi​ui​⟹A=UΣV⊤,

with U and V orthogonal and Σ diagonal. This holds for every real matrix, square or not, which is what makes the SVD the most informative factorisation in numerical linear algebra.

Derivation from AᵀA

Multiply A=UΣV⊤ by its transpose:

A⊤A=VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤=VΣ2V⊤.

That is an eigendecomposition. So the vi​ are eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix A⊤A, the singular values are the square roots of its eigenvalues, and then ui​=Avi​/σi​.

This route squares the condition number, like the normal equations, so production codes avoid forming A⊤A. The one-sided Jacobi method instead rotates pairs of columns of A until they are mutually orthogonal; the column norms are then the singular values. It is short to write and accurate.

What the SVD tells you:

  • σ1​=∥A∥2​ is the largest stretch, and σ1​/σn​ is the condition number (lesson 13).
  • The number of nonzero σi​ is the rank.
  • For a robot Jacobian, σi​ are the tip speeds per unit joint speed along the manipulability ellipse’s axes; a zero singular value is a singularity.

Worked example

A=(34​05​), so A⊤A=(2520​2025​).

  1. Eigenvalues of A⊤A: 25±20, so 45 and 5.
  2. σ1​=45​=6.708, σ2​=5​=2.236.
  3. Eigenvectors: v1​=(1,1)/2​, v2​=(1,−1)/2​.
  4. u1​=Av1​/σ1​=(3,9)/(2​⋅6.708)=(0.3162,0.9487).
  5. Checks: σ1​σ2​=15=∣detA∣, and κ=6.708/2.236=3.

Code it from scratch

svd.py
import numpy as np

def svd_via_eig(A):
    A = np.asarray(A, float)
    w, V = np.linalg.eigh(A.T @ A)              # symmetric eigensolver (see lesson 11 for Jacobi)
    idx = np.argsort(w)[::-1]; w, V = w[idx], V[:, idx]
    s = np.sqrt(np.clip(w, 0, None))
    U = (A @ V) / s
    return U, s, V

def svd_jacobi(A, tol=1e-14, sweeps=60):
    U = np.array(A, float); n = U.shape[1]; V = np.eye(n)
    for _ in range(sweeps):
        rotated = False
        for p in range(n - 1):
            for q in range(p + 1, n):
                a, b = U[:, p] @ U[:, p], U[:, q] @ U[:, q]
                g = U[:, p] @ U[:, q]
                if abs(g) <= tol * np.sqrt(a * b): continue
                rotated = True
                zeta = (b - a) / (2 * g)
                t = np.sign(zeta) / (abs(zeta) + np.sqrt(1 + zeta ** 2)) if zeta != 0 else 1.0
                c = 1 / np.sqrt(1 + t * t); s = c * t
                for M in (U, V):
                    Mp, Mq = M[:, p].copy(), M[:, q].copy()
                    M[:, p], M[:, q] = c * Mp - s * Mq, s * Mp + c * Mq
        if not rotated: break
    sig = np.linalg.norm(U, axis=0)
    idx = np.argsort(sig)[::-1]
    return U[:, idx] / sig[idx], sig[idx], V[:, idx]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    U, s, V = svd_via_eig([[3, 0], [4, 5]])
    assert np.allclose(s, [45 ** .5, 5 ** .5]) and np.allclose(abs(U[:, 0]), [0.31623, 0.94868], atol=1e-5)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
    for shape in [(5, 3), (8, 8), (12, 4)]:
        A = rng.standard_normal(shape)
        for f in (svd_via_eig, svd_jacobi):
            U, s, V = f(A)
            assert np.allclose(U @ np.diag(s) @ V.T, A, atol=1e-10)
            assert np.allclose(s, np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False), rtol=1e-9)
    print("both SVDs reconstruct A and match NumPy's singular values")

Exercises

Find the singular values of diag(3,−2).

Show the solution

A⊤A=diag(9,4), so σ=3,2. Singular values are never negative; the sign moves into U (here u2​=−e2​).

A 6-joint robot’s 6 × 6 Jacobian has singular values 1.2, 0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1 and 0.002 (in m/s per rad/s or rad/s per rad/s). What does that tell you?

Show the solution
  1. The condition number is 1.2/0.002=600: the arm is close to a singularity.
  2. Along the direction u6​ the tip moves only 0.002 units per unit joint speed, so commanding motion there needs huge joint speeds. A controller should slow down or use damped least squares (Phase 07).

toc.title: Every matrix maps a circle to an ellipse

quiz.q: What is the largest singular value of (34​05​)?
quiz.explain: The eigenvalues of A⊤A are 45 and 5, so σ1​=45​=6.708.

quiz.q: What is the condition number σ1​/σ2​ of the same matrix?
quiz.explain: 45​/5​=9​=3.

quiz.q: The right singular vectors V of A are…
quiz.explain: A⊤A=VΣ2V⊤ is an eigendecomposition.

quiz.q: How many nonzero singular values does a 4 × 3 matrix of rank 2 have?
quiz.explain: The rank equals the number of nonzero singular values.

quiz.q: For a 2 × 2 matrix with singular values 4 and 0.5, what is ∣detA∣?
quiz.explain: ∣detA∣=σ1​σ2​ because rotations have determinant ±1.
